title: Preventable vs Non-Preventable Denials Management
summary: Learn to classify and manage denials, identify root causes, and prioritize actions for maximum impact in healthcare revenue cycle management.
body_markdown:
*By Vanessa C*


**Summary:** Preventable denials in revenue cycle management require corrective actions such as root-cause analysis and workflow changes, while non-preventable denials need monitoring and baseline tracking to identify changes. Effective management involves understanding the root causes, assigning ownership for payer communications, and separating denials into preventable and non-preventable categories to allocate resources efficiently and maximize impact.


An 835 remittance file shows up with CARC 197 for missing pre-certification, while another batch lands under CARC 96 for non-covered charges tied to an unannounced commercial plan policy update. Both write-offs hit the patient accounting system as denied balances, but treating them with the same workflow eats staff time and leaves cash behind. Revenue cycle teams often fall back on broad front-end prevention work, yet denial reduction starts when the organization separates claims it could have stopped from those driven by payer behavior outside its control. Distinguishing between preventable and non-preventable denials management gives the operational clarity needed to stop repeat technical errors at registration while still pushing clinical payment disputes through targeted appeals and contract enforcement.


Initial denial volume still strains hospital margins nationwide. A[2024 Health Affairs analysis found Medicare Advantage plans deny 17 percent of initial claims](https://www.healthaffairs.org/doi/10.1377/hlthaff.2024.01485) , while[KFF reported in 2024 that ACA Marketplace insurers denied nearly 19 percent of in-network claims](https://www.kff.org/patient-consumer-protections/claims-denials-and-appeals-in-aca-marketplace-plans-in-2024/) . If these rejections stay mixed together, patient financial services teams spend payroll on accounts that will never pay and let avoidable administrative write-offs pile up.


## Start With Root Cause, Not the Denial Category


CARC and RARC codes explain why an insurer refused payment, but they rarely point to the operational miss. A denial mapped under authorization may look purely operational at first glance. If patient access failed to send clinical documentation before an elective surgery, that write-off is fully preventable.


If the surgical team secured prior authorization, followed the documented utilization criteria, and the payer later changed clinical review rules after discharge without notice, the root cause sits outside hospital control. According to a[2024 Becker's Payer report tracking hospital claims processing trends](https://www.beckerspayer.com/payer/claims-denial-rates-up-prior-auth-denials-down-in-2024-report/) , overall claim denial rates rose even as prior authorization denials saw slight declines, which shows how shifting adjudication patterns make front-end resolution harder.


Assigning true preventability means auditing what happened right after an administrative or policy update:


1. Did the payer publish an updated medical policy bulletin, and did your billing office record the receipt?
2. Did your practice management system keep an automated edit that held the affected claim before release?
3. Did clinical documentation confirm medical necessity under the contract terms active on the date of service?


If the system held usable knowledge that staff failed to apply, label the denial preventable. If the payer carried out an unannounced retro-adjudication, classify it as non-preventable.


## Someone Should Own Payer Change Management


Payer policy updates arrive constantly through regional portals, provider bulletins, and clearinghouse circulars. Without a named owner, those rule changes create quiet administrative rejections across high-volume service lines.


Set up a payer change coordinator, RCM liaison, or operational review desk whose job is watching incoming policy changes. This role tracks portal updates, reviews clearinghouse payer alerts, and works across registration, coding, and billing units to turn written policy revisions into EHR claim scrubbers.


When a payer changes billing guidelines without direct notice, the coordinator must record the effective date and build an audit trail. Having documented proof of unnotified policy adjustments gives managed care teams leverage during joint operating committee reviews and turns what looks like internal billing error into clear payer non-compliance.


## Separate Preventable and Non-Preventable Denials


Preventable and non-preventable inventory serve different operational functions in hospital revenue cycle management:


- Preventable rejections point to internal breakdowns across scheduling, patient access, coding accuracy, and credentialing. They call for corrective action plans, staff re-education, updated front-end edits, and process audits.
- Non-preventable rejections measure external friction, including unpredictable medical necessity audits, unannounced clinical guideline shifts, and payer system adjudication errors.


Managing these groups together muddies performance metrics. If total denials spike by 15 percent, directors need to know right away whether patient access missed primary coverage validation or whether one payer applied a retroactive payment algorithm to inpatient stays. Tracking each group separately points operational remediation toward internal root causes and keeps external payer trends set aside for appeal teams and contract negotiators.


The exception to this split occurs in clinical trials and emergency department EMTALA presentations: services provided under emergency stabilization mandates or experimental protocols cannot be changed by front-end rules, so traditional preventability scoring loses value for these specialty claims.


## Know Exactly What the Denial Dollars Represent


Executive dashboards frequently blur denial exposure by reporting gross billed charges alongside actual financial loss. A $10 million denial total reported in gross charges can obscure the actual cash risk depending on the hospital's reimbursement yields under contracted commercial fee schedules.


Metric Type Operational Definition Best Applied For Reporting Pitfall to Avoid


Gross Billed Charges Total chargemaster rate submitted on the initial UB-04 or CMS-1500 Enterprise intake auditing and overall billing volume tracking Overstates real cash exposure to executive leadership


Expected Net Reimbursement Contracted allowable amount expected based on payer fee schedules Operational prioritization, appeal queues, and cash impact Miscalculates true revenue if contract modeling tables lag


Net Final Write-Offs Claim balance transferred to contractual or administrative adjustment Historical loss reviews and financial ledger reporting Lagging indicator that fails to flag active AR risk


Always report denial balances based on expected net revenue rather than gross charge sums. Aligning these numbers makes sure patient accounting managers allocate follow-up resources toward accounts carrying real cash value.


## Look at Both Volume and Financial Impact


Effective denial reduction evaluates claim frequency alongside dollar magnitude. High-dollar surgical rejections require direct clinical appeal even at very low claim volumes, as writing off a single inpatient case damages margin targets.


At the same time, high-volume rejections for low-dollar technical items—such as missing modifier 25 or incorrect primary payer identification—drain collector productivity. Operational research from[TechTarget RevCycleIntelligence breaking down payer denial patterns](https://www.techtarget.com/revcyclemanagement/feature/Breaking-down-claim-denial-rates-by-healthcare-payer) emphasizes how high-frequency administrative denials systematically stall provider cash flow when left unaddressed. Repeated small rejections each month can add up to significant delayed revenue, which can be reduced through effective clearinghouse scrubber rules.


Use an impact matrix to route accounts:


\[High Volume / Low Dollar\] –> Deploy Automated Scrubbers & Staff Edits \[High Volume / High Dollar\] –> Executive Intervention & Enterprise Root-Cause Work \[Low Volume / Low Dollar\] –> Bulk Resolution & Periodic Clearinghouse Drops \[Low Volume / High Dollar\] –> Specialist Clinical Review & Level-Two Appeals


## Look Across the Revenue Cycle Before Fixing One Area


Isolating a denial fix to one billing department often masks systemic issues spanning the wider revenue cycle. If an oncology clinic registers a steep rise in authorization rejections, the default reaction is auditing that clinic's administrative coordinators.


However, an enterprise audit might reveal that central scheduling routed off-campus infusion orders through an intake workflow that bypassed authorization verification entirely. Focusing entirely on clinic clerks fails to resolve the upstream scheduling gap affecting ambulatory surgery, cardiology, and radiology.


Before revising departmental procedures, query enterprise billing records for identical CARC, RARC, and remark codes across all provider departments. If the pattern spans two or more distinct clinical service lines, redesign the central operational process rather than retraining front-desk staff in one silo.


## When the Issue Is Enterprise-Wide, Use an Enterprise Plan


Systemic denial spikes crossing multiple facilities demand central administrative coordination. When root causes extend into enterprise workflows, deploy a standardized remediation protocol:


1. Hard-stop the error at intake by implementing mandatory patient accounting fields or automated eligibility verification triggers.
2. Update clearinghouse scrubbers to hold outbound 837 claim files matching the identified failure criteria before claims reach the payer.
3. Isolate existing unbilled and denied inventory associated with the defect into dedicated work queues for bulk correction.
4. Establish weekly executive reconciliation until the trailing 30-day denial rate for that root cause falls below baseline targets.


Stopping the incoming error pattern protects future billings, allowing accounts receivable follow-up teams to focus entirely on existing timely filing limits for stranded inventory.


## Protect Recoverability First


The odds of collecting on an unhedged unpaid balance drop day after day while an account sits idle. Insurance companies write rigid filing deadlines into their contracts, often restricting secondary reviews to 60, 90, or 180 days following that first 835 remittance date. Once those clocks run out, the money vanishes.


Sort your appeal queues around hard contractual deadlines instead of sorting by gross dollar amounts or the alphabet:


- Claims approaching final contractual appeal limits within 15 calendar days sit at the top of the working list.
- High-dollar inpatient claims facing standard 60-day deadlines go to staff immediately after those urgent accounts.
- High-volume administrative rejections requiring standard clearinghouse resubmission follow behind the inpatient reviews.


Software can speed up routine status checks so billers spend their hours actually working accounts. For health systems that contract out claim-statusing and AR collections,[LunaBill](https://lunabill.com/) brings in 13 specialized AI agents that log into portals like Availity and Waystar, place outbound payer phone calls, read denial codes, and write appeal letters directly inside EHR platforms such as Epic and Cerner.


When teams group similar claims together by payer and denial code, billers stop hopping between mismatched portals all morning. That focus lets them push appeals out before statutory deadlines expire.


## Non-Preventable Does Not Mean Non-Actionable


Putting a denial in the non-preventable column should never prompt billing staff to write the balance off. Many of these rejections stem from incorrect adjudication rules, downcoding algorithms, or internal payer medical necessity reviews running in direct violation of the actual contract terms.


A[2024 STAT News investigation on health plan claim denial practices](https://www.statnews.com/2024/05/01/insurance-claim-denials-compromise-patient-care-provider-bottom-lines/) showed how random commercial claim denials eat directly into hospital margins and called on health systems to dispute illegitimate balance rejections.


Collect the remittance records whenever a pattern of non-preventable denials shows up. Send that package straight to Managed Care Contracting. Calculate the total dollars withheld, point out where medical charts satisfied the exact contractual definitions, and demand that the insurer reprocess the disputed claims through administrative settlements at quarterly joint operating committee meetings.


## Establish a Baseline for Expected Non-Preventable Denials


Every hospital deals with a base layer of unavoidable claim friction. Commercial coordination of benefits updates, for instance, cannot proceed until the patient picks up the phone and speaks with the insurer directly. A functional revenue cycle operation tracks these friction points by setting clear acceptable limits. Measure non-preventable claims as a proportion of monthly remittance volume. Run formal operational reviews on these claim categories once every quarter. If that share stays within expected historic ranges, daily operations can continue as planned.


Surges beyond that historical limit demand an operational audit right away. When supposedly unpreventable rejections shoot upward, the cause is almost always an unannounced edit update by the payer, revised adjudication logic inside their clearinghouse, or a quiet registration failure inside the hospital that looked like an external rule change.


## A Practical Leadership Framework


### Define Preventability


Mark a denial as preventable only when registration or billing employees had clear information, operational tools, and sufficient advance warning to stop the error prior to claim submission.


### Separate the Buckets


Split preventable and non-preventable balances across two independent tracking dashboards so clinic managers can repair registration workflows while appeal specialists focus on commercial payer friction.


### Define the Metrics


Calculate denial figures using expected net revenue rather than inflated chargemaster figures so revenue cycle directors can evaluate cash risk accurately.


### Prioritize by Volume and Impact


Route large inpatient claim files straight to senior clinical appeal nurses, and remove repeated low-dollar technical errors by turning on automated claim edits at the front end.


### Look for the Broader Pattern


Review billing figures across all hospital facilities and ambulatory clinics before treating a repeated denial as a localized problem tied to one registration desk.


### Stop the Source


Resolve data entry problems inside scheduling, patient registration, and coding before pulling billers away to resolve aging accounts receivable balances.


### Protect Recoverability


Order appeal workflows around payer filing windows and contract deadlines to prevent permanent balance write-offs.


### Work the Impacted Population


Cluster disputed accounts by payer identification number, root cause, and electronic submission format so staff can send batch appeals and mass clearinghouse rebills quickly.


### Monitor Non-Preventable Denials


Establish reference baselines for unavoidable claims and start joint reviews whenever numbers shift outside historic bounds.


### Document and Reassess


Write down each insurer agreement, distribute clear billing policies across departments, and adjust preventability categories whenever contract terms or clearinghouse adjudication algorithms change.


## Focus the Work Where the Organization Can Make a Difference


Revenue cycle leaders should not treat every remittance rejection as an internal mistake. If a payer creates the problem, piling on the same corrective workflow only burns staff time and hides the real weak spots.


Put process fixes, staff training, and claim scrubbers on the errors the billing team can actually control. Track non-preventable denials as a separate stream, keep a baseline for them, and send stubborn payer disputes to contracting so earned reimbursement does not sit in limbo.

## Conclusion


Audit your active 835 remittance data from the last 90 days and pull out the top five CARC codes driving current accounts receivable balances. Trace each code back to the department where it started, then check whether staff had the operational data needed to stop the rejection before it happened.


Set up separate reporting paths for preventable and non-preventable inventory inside your practice management system. Put claim scrubber edits on preventable administrative issues first, and give accounts with firm appeal deadlines to senior recovery specialists. Keeping internal process controls apart from outside payer disputes cuts recurring billing leaks and protects net revenue performance across every patient encounter.
